I N T R O D U C T I O N
From Resources to Resilience
70th Integrated Annual Report 2025-26
NLC India Limited a

NLC India Limited a
It’s been nearly seven decades since we have been mining lignite to power the nation. Often dubbed ‘brown coal’, lignite is crucial as an abundant, low-cost, and reliable domestic fuel to produce electricity. As the country’s largest lignite miner, we have been serving India through every phase of its development.
Our Navratna status makes us responsive to an evolving market dynamics and keeps us responsible for India’s economic progress. Our commitment to the making of a developed India reflects in our resolve to stay in sync with the transition sweeping through the power sector. While keeping the core intact, we are building our renewable capacity steadily, holding firm on the reliability the country depends on.
This steady shift towards renewables makes the theme for this year's annual report. The document reflects the dynamism of a company that is stepping up, gaining pace and building strength for the road ahead.
At NLC India, we define resilience as the ability to prepare for tomorrow based on today’s performance. We are running our mines and power stations at their best and, at the same time, raising our renewable capacity and opening new lines of growth in energy storage, critical minerals and clean technologies.

This momentum draws on the financial strength that funds our growth, the capability and the drive of our people, the research and partnerships that carry us from a resource base to create value for our stakeholders and build their confidence in us. These forces complement one another, keeping us resilient and in step with a rapidly changing landscape.

This report covers the period from April 1, 2025 to March 31, 2026 and as on date presents an integrated view of the NLCIL Group, taking in its Subsidiaries, Associates and Joint Ventures. As on date the Group comprises 5 Subsidiaries, 2 Joint Ventures and 4 Step-down Subsidiary Companies, as listed below.
NLC India Limited (NLCIL) is proud to present its fifth Integrated Annual Report, setting out a complete account of how the Company has performed across financial and non-financial dimensions during FY 2025-26. Through these pages, we share the milestones reached, the ground covered, initiatives carried forward during the year and as on date providing our stakeholders with the clarity they need to form their own judgements. The report reflects our continuing endeavour to build enduring value and conduct our business responsibly as the energy sector around us continues to evolve.

Every operational site within NLCIL applies a common and clearly defined method to gather, measure, compute and examine its performance data. Holding to a single approach across locations gives our disclosures their accuracy and consistency, and allows management to plan and decide on a dependable footing.
The account presented here brings together the financial and non-financial dimensions of the Group's performance. Our financial results, on both a standalone and a consolidated basis, have been examined in detail by M/s. Sundaram & Srinivasan, Chartered Accountants and M/s. PKF Sridhar & Santhanam LLP, Chartered Accountants. Engaging two audit firms lends added assurance to the reliability of the financial information we place on record.
Placing accurate and complete information before our stakeholders, covering financial, Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) and operational performance alike, remains an obligation we take seriously. This report has taken shape through wide consultation with business units and departments across the organisation, supported by the guidance of those charged with governance. Responsibility for the integrity, objectivity, transparency and fair presentation of what appears in these pages rests jointly with the Board and the Management.

INTRODUCTION
MESSAGE FROM THE CHAIRMAN & MANAGING DIRECTOR
A Year of Record Performance

A Year of Record Performance
Market capitalisation touched ₹53,774 crore. We achieved 100% collection efficiency from our power beneficiaries and maintained a consistent record of dividend declarations since 1998-99. Capital expenditure of ₹9,131 crore, the highest ever, demonstrates our determination to accelerate capacity creation and strategic growth.
The resource is the foundation of our business, and resilience is what we are building on top of it: a wider geography, lignite and coal as fuel, solar and wind as energy, and storage for supply.
FY 2025-26 has been one of the most successful years in NLCIL's history. Your Company achieved its highest-ever annual coal production of 19.14 million tonnes and highest-ever coal dispatch of 17.69 million tonnes since inception. Total power generation stood at 28.94 Billion Units, while renewable energy generation reached an all-time high of 2.26 Billion Units. These achievements reflect our sustained focus on operational excellence, improved asset utilisation and greater efficiency across our businesses. The Company also added 1 GW of generating capacity during the year, further strengthening its position for future growth.
Strengthening the Mining Foundation

Strengthening the Mining Foundation
Mining remains a key pillar of our integrated energy model. Talabira-II & III OCP achieved its highest-ever single-day coal production and dispatch; Mine-II recorded its highest-ever annual lignite dispatch of 13.85 million tonnes; and Pachwara South OCP commenced coal production in March 2026. Significant progress was also made in Machhakata (Revised), New Patrapara South and North Dhadu Western Part coal projects.
Consolidated revenue from operations crossed ₹17,490 crore and Profit After Tax reached an all-time high of ₹3,769 crore.
Dear Shareholders,
Our mining excellence has been recognised through Five-Star Ratings from the Ministry of Coal, with NLCIL receiving a cumulative 23 Five-Star Ratings. We are also expanding into critical minerals, including phosphorite

It has been a year of strong operational performance, financial resilience, strategic expansion and accelerated progress towards building a diversified, future-ready energy enterprise.

As India advances towards the vision of Viksit Bharat @2047, the demand for reliable, affordable and sustainable energy is set to grow significantly. NLCIL is uniquely positioned to contribute to this national endeavour through its integrated strengths in mining, thermal power, renewable energy, emerging energy technologies and strategic resources. Our journey is evolving from that of a lignite mining and power generation company into a diversified energy enterprise with a growing pan-India presence.

ABOUT THE COMPANY
About the Company
OUR FOOTPRINT
NLC India at a Glance
NLC India Limited is a Navratna enterprise under the Ministry of Coal, Government of India. For close to seven decades, we have held a place at the centre of India’s energy story. Incorporated in 1956 to develop lignite reserves at Neyveli, we built something the country had not attempted before, which was a fully integrated mining and power complex. From that beginning, we have grown into an integrated energy enterprise, operating across 10 states and one Union Territory, with our corporate office at Neyveli in Tamil Nadu and registered office at Chennai.
10 States and 1 Union Territory where we operate

10 States and 1 Union Territory where we operate
Our integrated mine-to-megawatt model remains our defining strength. We mine the fuel, we generate the power, and we do both at a scale that keeps our costs contained and our supply secure. Pit head thermal stations sited alongside our own mines allow us to serve base load demand dependably, hour after hour, through seasons. It is a model that has earned the country's confidence and delivered 48 unbroken years of profitability and 26 consecutive years of dividend, a record few enterprises of our vintage can claim.
5 Mines 19 Operational power plants 9 Regional offices 9,735
That same pioneering instinct now carries us into a wider portfolio. We were the first Central Public Sector Enterprise in the country to cross a gigawatt of solar capacity, and we are building towards 10,110 MW of renewable capacity by 2030. Alongside this, we have entered battery energy storage, secured two critical mineral blocks in Chhattisgarh, and begun work on a green hydrogen facility at Neyveli. Seven decades on, our purpose stands where it always has, which is to create wealth for well-being.

ABOUT THE COMPANY
Our Business Portfolio
NLCIL is built around three businesses that feed one another. We mine lignite and coal, we convert that fuel into power at stations built alongside the mines, and we generate clean energy from the sun and the wind across the country. Around this core sits a growing set of newer businesses, taking us into energy storage, critical minerals and green hydrogen. What binds the portfolio together is its integration: fuel raised from our own mines feeds our own plants, and the earnings from that dependable core fund our move into cleaner sources.

ABOUT THE COMPANY
EMERGING BUSINESSES
THERMAL POWER

THERMAL POWER
Beyond generation, we have begun building revenue lines that draw on what we already know and already hold. Our overburden is being converted into manufactured sand through a plant of 1.0 MTPA commissioned at Mine I in February 2026, with commercial sale already under way. We have been declared the successful bidder for the Semhardih and Raipura phosphorite and limestone blocks in Chhattisgarh, carrying 1 MTPA each, and we are working with the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre and Indian Rare Earths Limited on extracting rare earth elements, including from our own fly ash. NLCIL Secured Two critical mineral blocks viz., Parvathapur Block and Govindpur Block in Sangareddy district of Telangana having deposits of Vanadium, Titanium, and Aluminous Laterite.
During the year we commenced commercial operation of Unit II of the Ghatampur Thermal Power Project, adding 660 MW and taking Neyveli Uttar Pradesh Power Limited to 1,320 MW. Our thermal stations supplied power to beneficiary states across the country and continued to provide the round the clock reliability that solar and wind cannot yet deliver on their own.

We operate 6,620 MW of installed thermal capacity, of which 3,640 MW sits directly with us and 2,980 MW with our joint venture companies, NLC Tamil Nadu Power Limited and Neyveli Uttar Pradesh Power Limited. Our stations at Neyveli and Barsingsar benefit from a pit-head lignite arrangement, significantly reducing long-distance fuel transportation and the associated emissions. This integrated mine-to-power model ensures reliable fuel supply, improves operational efficiency, reduces fuel logistics and transportation-related carbon footprint, and supports NLCIL’s broader climate action and decarbonisation efforts.

OUR SUBSIDIARIES AND JOINT VENTURES
RENEWABLE POWER
We deliver through a group structure that gives each business the focus it needs. NLC India Renewables Limited holds and grows our renewable portfolio and is being prepared for a public listing. NLC India Green Energy Limited manages our diversification businesses. NLC Tamil Nadu Power Limited and Neyveli Uttar Pradesh Power Limited operate our joint venture thermal capacity, and NLC Rajasthan Power Limited carries our lignite-based Thermal Power Project in the state of Rajasthan. Coal Lignite Urja Vikas Private Limited is our joint venture with Coal India Limited. Four step down subsidiaries under NLC India Renewables Limited, namely NIRL Assam Renewables Limited, NIRL Rajasthan Renewables Limited, NIRL NCRTC Renewables Limited and NIRL OREDA Renewables Limited are taking our renewable presence in the State of Assam, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh, respectively.

ABOUT THE COMPANY
Governance
Sound governance has anchored the way we create value at NLC India Limited. As a Navratna enterprise, we work at the meeting point of public purpose and commercial discipline, with the governance framework built to carry both. In a year when we widened our presence across mining, thermal power, renewables, energy storage, critical minerals and emerging clean energy businesses, that framework gave our diversification the structure, the oversight and the accountability it needed. We celebrated our Raising day on 26th May, 2026, and the confidence placed in us by the Government of India State Government, Regulators, Discoms, JV Partners, Trade Unions, Associations our regulators, and more than 3 lakh shareholders continue to shape how we govern.
Risk Management and Internal Controls

Risk Management and Internal Controls
As a Government Company, the remuneration of our Board- level Directors is fixed by the Government of India as the appointing authority, while the remuneration of our executives and non-unionised supervisors follows the guidelines of the Department of Public Enterprises, and the wages and service conditions of our workmen are governed by settlements with the recognised trade unions.
We predict, pre-empt, and prevent risks through a structured, Board-supervised framework. The Risk Management Committee at the Board level, supported by various panels under the Board of Directors, identifies, evaluates and monitors the risks facing the Company and charts out the mitigation strategy. The risks can be both external and internal. Our internal control systems, reviewed by the Audit Committee and tested by internal and statutory audit, give the Board the assurance that our assets are safeguarded and our reporting is reliable. As we diversify into new businesses and geographies, this framework helps us take considered risks while protecting the interests of our stakeholders.

The scope of our Nomination and Remuneration Committee is limited to matters below Board level, where it considers and recommends performance related pay in line with those guidelines. Our remuneration is therefore not linked directly to environmental, social and governance performance indicators.
Ethics, Integrity and Compliance
As a Government Company we are also exempt, under circulars of the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, from the provisions of the Companies Act governing the manner of performance evaluation of the Board, its Committees and individual Directors, and from the corresponding provisions of Schedule IV relating to Independent Directors, where the administrative Ministry specifies the evaluation framework.
Integrity guides how we operate. We run the business under a Code of Conduct that applies to our Board members and the senior management personnel. We maintain strict vigil to ensure transparency and accountability across the organisation. Our procurement and investment decisions follow established, transparent processes, including participation in competitive bidding and public auctions for renewable capacity, coal and critical mineral blocks. We meet our statutory and regulatory obligations by following guidelines laid out by the Companies Act and the SEBI Regulations, and by making timely and accurate disclosures.
Stakeholders and Investors

Stakeholders and Investors
We engage our shareholders and the wider investor community with openness and regularity. During the year, we hosted institutional investor interactions, including our Q2 and Q4 FY 2025-26 Institutional Investors Meet at Mumbai, where our leadership presented the Company's performance, strategy and outlook and responded to questions directly. With a shareholder base of more than three lakh, a record of dividends sustained over 26 years and profitability over 48 years, we treat clear, two-way communication as central to the trust we hold.
We reinforce this through our Integrity Pact programme, implemented with the Central Vigilance Commission and Transparency International India, which forms part of our procurement process and applies to every tender above ₹1 crore. The framework extends to our employees, suppliers, contractors, consultants, joint ventures and subsidiaries. During FY 2025-26 we conducted awareness and training programmes on anti-corruption, ethical business conduct and the prevention of anti-competitive practices, ran sessions on regulatory change and compliance requirements, and strengthened our enterprise risk management practices to identify and mitigate governance and compliance risks.
Governance in a Year of Strategic Change

Governance in a Year of Strategic Change
During the year under review, we took some significant strategic steps, and our governance held firm through each of them. Our Board and the relevant authorities approved the transfer of renewable assets to NLC India Renewables Limited, a wholly Owned Subsidiary and an alternative mechanism for its listing. Cleared the formation of joint ventures for nuclear generation with NPCIL and for renewable capacity with NCRTC, and oversaw capacity additions and new project approvals across the portfolio.
Our Governance Framework
Familiarisation of Independent Directors
Our governance structure has the Board of Directors at its apex, supported by specialised committees and a professional management team. As a Central Public Sector Enterprise with the Government of India controlling 69.47% stake, we are accountable to the as Ministry of Coal, our Shareholders and other stakeholders. We govern in line with the Companies Act, 2013, the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, and the Guidelines on Corporate Governance for Central Public Sector Enterprises issued by the Department of Public Enterprises.

We recognise that effective independent oversight rests on a clear understanding of our business. Our structured familiarisation process helps the independent directors align with the Company’s vision and mission, make them aware of our profile and subsidiaries, our mining and power operations, our present capacity across mines and power stations, and our production and financial performance. During the reporting year, familiarisation extended to the priorities shaping our next phase of growth, including our Corporate Plan 2030, our capacity addition programme across thermal and renewable energy, our entry into energy storage and critical minerals, and our research and development initiatives with leading national institutions. The directors are also briefed on their roles, duties and responsibilities, and on the evolving regulatory environment.
Policies and Disclosures
We have a framework of Board-approved policies that supports consistent and compliant conduct across the Company, including our policies on related-party transactions, material events, document preservation and website disclosure. In keeping with the Regulation 30 of the SEBI Listing Regulations, we disclose material events and other information on our website and retain them for the periods set out in our Archival Policy, so that our stakeholders have access to the information.

This layered structure keeps our decision-making transparent, distributes responsibility clearly, and allows independent oversight of a business that spans several states and multiple energy verticals.

Reducing Environmental Impact of Thermal Power

Reducing Environmental Impact of Thermal Power
The year also brought recognition for how we mine and new ways of selling what we produce. The Ministry of Coal has now conferred 23 Five-Star Ratings on our coal and lignite operations, and for FY 2023-24 it rated Mine-IA, Talabira II and III and Barsingsar at five stars and Mine-I and Mine-II at four. We migrated the e-auction of lignite, coal, minor minerals and overburden from an outsourced platform to our own NeAT portal, and we introduced special long-term auctions with a validity of 360 days to give our customers greater certainty of supply. We became the first in India to commercialise the sale of overburden, from Mine-IA, and of washed silica sand, from Mine-I. The Government of Tamil Nadu has approved the disposal of overburden soil from our external dumps and its conversion into manufactured sand for a period of ten years, extending the circular-economy work described in our Natural Capital.

Our renewable portfolio is the fastest-growing part of our asset base, and it is central to the diversification of our Manufactured Capital. During FY 2025-26, our renewable energy generation reached an all-time high of 2.26 billion units, and we added 352.80 MW of renewable capacity to the group. Our operational renewable capacity stood at 1,785 MW as on date with a substantial portfolio under implementation, positioning renewables as a defining element of our future generation mix.

Our mining operations supply the fuel that underpins our thermal generation, and FY 2025-26 was a year of contrast across our two fuels. Our coal production at Talabira reached an all-time high of 19.14 million tonnes, up from 17.20 million tonnes, and coal despatch from the same project reached 17.69 million tonnes, also the highest since the project began. We commenced production at our Pachwara South coal block during the year, strengthening the fuel security of our power portfolio and adding good-quality coal for sale in the open market over and above our own requirement. Our lignite production stood at 21.27 million tonnes in line with the fuel demands of the linked end use plants, lower than the 24.06 million tonnes of the previous year, reflecting a planned shift in output across our Neyveli mines as our fuel mix changes. Overburden removal at Mine-II reached 94.38 million cubic metres, the highest the mine has recorded.

We are progressively lowering the environmental impact of our thermal generation while continuing to supply reliable electricity. We are doing so through the adoption of high-efficiency power generation technologies, biomass co-firing, and advanced emission control systems, and through our carbon capture research with IIT Madras. We practise scientific fly ash management and the recovery of critical minerals from ash, integrate renewable energy, conserve water, and apply digital optimisation and robust environmental management systems across our operations. Together, these measures support India's transition towards cleaner and more sustainable energy, and they connect this capital directly to the research described in our Intellectual Capital and the stewardship discussed in our Natural Capital.
Building Towards 2030
We have framed our asset strategy with the idea of reaching a balanced and resilient portfolio by 2030. We are working towards a mining capacity of around 104 million tonnes per annum, and more than 10GW each of thermal and renewable capacities that would drive us towards a balanced mix of electricity. In this way, the infrastructure we build today, from our modernised thermal stations to our expanding renewables fleet, turns our resource base into lasting resilience, and carries the strength of our past into the energy system of the future.

Green Hydrogen Initiatives
The geopolymer bricks made of fly ash and overburden sand offer a sustainable alternative to conventional building material. Cured using solar heating, instead of traditional kiln firing, these bricks significantly reduce energy consumption and carbon emissions, lowering the carbon footprint of the construction industry. This innovation advanced to a filed patent in April 2025.
Our exploration of green hydrogen has moved from intent to execution. We are extending this work into alternative pathways, including biohydrogen from biomass, pursued with Alagappa University, and renewable hydrogen from biogas through solar-driven methane cracking, pursued with Annamalai University.

Learning, Development and Well-being
At NLCIL, we are deeply committed towards supporting our employees throughout their careers and even after retirement. To ensure a smooth transition, our Learning and Development Centre hosts monthly sessions tailored for employees approaching retirement. These sessions provide comprehensive information about the Post-Retirement Medical Assistance (PRMA), Post-Retirement Medical Insurance (PRMI) and the NLCIL Pension Schemes. Through these informative programmes, we ensure that employees are fully informed about the health and financial benefits available to them after retirement. By offering clear guidance on how to navigate these provisions, we empower our employees to make well-informed decisions regarding their medical and financial security post-retirement. Our goal is to equip our employees with the knowledge and tools required to ensure their well-being and peace of mind during their retirement years.
Building a Future-ready Workforce

Building a Future-ready Workforce
Learning is how we prepare our people for the journey ahead, and in FY 2025-26 we widened its scale and reach considerably. Through our Learning and Development Centre, we conducted 2,012 programmes over 3,662 training days, reaching out to 39,778 participants and covering 51,555 man-days, an average of about 26 participants for every programme. This growth in both volume and coverage reflects a stronger organisational emphasis on continuous learning as our business diversifies.
Our core training programmes covered 10,398 participants across behavioural competencies, health and well-being, functional and statutory areas, and apprentice training, with behavioural competency programmes alone reaching 3,478 people. Our specialised interventions covered a further 29,380 participants, led by skill upgrade, which made up 400 programmes and 8,121 participants, close to two-thirds of that segment. Functional-technology, mining, management development and onboarding made up much of the remainder, showing that our learning responds to operational and technical needs as they arise.

Safety in Our Mines Our mining safety rests on prevention built into the operation itself. We practise blast-free lignite mining across our Neyveli mines using bucket wheel excavators with belt conveyors and spreaders, and blast-free methods at Barsingsar and, for coal extraction, at Talabira through surface miners. Every item of heavy earth-moving machinery is fitted with an Automatic Fire Detection and Suppression System. We have prepared Safety Management Plans for all six mines under the Coal Mines Regulations 2017, based on hazard identification and risk assessment, and we review them every six months.
Safety in Our Thermal Stations

Safety in Our Thermal Stations
We ensure safety in our thermal power stations through disciplined operating practices. We enforce strict use of personal protective equipment, carry out routine inspections with immediate corrective action, and conduct toolbox talks before work begins. We have prepared and implemented 600 standard operating procedures for operation and maintenance works, and our stations are subject to external safety audit by the National Safety Council every two years, with observations acted upon in full.
Health and Safety
Safety as a Foremost Priority
Safety is inseparable from how we mine lignite and generate power. Across our mines, coal operations and thermal stations, we protect our people through engineered controls, disciplined systems and a culture of shared responsibility. In FY 2025-26, that commitment reflected in our safety performance.
To suppress dust, we deploy 30 water sprinklers and six fog cannons across our mines, supported by road-sweeping machines and motor graders for haul-road maintenance, and we monitor respirable dust and ambient air quality continuously.
Assurance, Technology and Medical Care

Assurance, Technology and Medical Care
We assure our safety through regular audit and continuous improvements. Our mines undergo internal safety audit by Corporate Safety every year, and Safety and Health Management System audits are conducted and uploaded to the National Coal Mines Safety Report portal in line with Ministry of Coal guidelines. Our NLCIL Aran mobile safety app allows our people to report unsafe observations and near misses for prompt compliance, extending safety awareness to the frontline. Our medical care underpins all of this: initial and periodical medical examinations for everyone engaged in the mines, free cardiac screening for all employees, medical officers trained in ILO chest x-ray classification to detect dust-related illness early, and a first- aid station with an ambulance at every mine and thermal station.

Discipline at the mine gate matters as much as engineering. No one enters a mine, whether our own employee or a contractor's, without an initial medical examination, basic vocational training at our Group Vocational Training Centre under the Mines Vocational Training Rules 1966, and a valid entry pass, which CISF personnel check at the single entrance every working shift. We have framed separate standard operating procedures for women employed in the mines. We have conducted scientific studies of slope stability in all our mines under the Coal Mines Regulations 2017 and implemented the recommendations, prepared crisis management plans for every mine, carry out noise surveys in line with DGMS guidance, maintain illumination at the prescribed levels, and have banned mobile phones in working areas in favour of walkie-talkies. On our conveyors, pre-start sirens and public address announcements in the local language, audio-visual blinkers along the belt and lock-out indicator lamps warn our people before machinery moves.

We also drew a direct line from education to livelihood. Water security ran through much of our FY 2025-26 work, addressed from both ends: getting clean water to people, and replenishing the resource itself. We built potable water schemes in the Jharsuguda and Sambalpur districts of Odisha, restored the Manimuktha River, rejuvenated traditional tanks and ponds, and constructed check dams, overhead tanks and village water infrastructure. Together these improved access to safe water, recharged groundwater and supported the sustainable use of a scarce resource in regions where water shapes daily life.

Health was where our community work reached the farthest in FY 2025-26, touching more than 4,52,000 lives. We treated the general public without charge through our General Hospital at Neyveli, and we strengthened public health institutions where they were most stretched. Our significant intervention addressed infant and maternal mortality in Cuddalore district. Working with the district administration and the Government Medical College Hospital, we provided advanced neonatal and obstetric equipment to the hospital and to government facilities across the district. The result was stronger emergency care for mothers and newborns, and a demonstration of what convergence between a public enterprise, a health department and a district administration can achieve for public health outcomes.

The reach was measurable. The rejuvenation of minor-irrigation tanks in Cuddalore benefitted 22,318 people, and RO plants and drinking water infrastructure reached more than 2,200 rural residents in Ariyalur.

Natural Capital
Managing greenhouse gases
Carbon capture research
We are also pursuing carbon capture at source, the harder part of the emissions problem for a thermal generator. Our research collaboration with the Indian Institute of Technology, Madras, established through a binding Memorandum of Understanding in May 2025 and fully funded by us, will be moving from a laboratory-scale study towards a pilot demonstration under Phase-II, and it reflects our intent to tackle carbon dioxide from combustion directly rather than through offsets alone.
We recognise our responsibility to limit greenhouse gas emissions and align with the nation's climate goals. As a power generator relying significantly on lignite, we account for our emissions and work towards bringing down their intensity as our clean energy capacity grows, through efficiency improvements, clean technologies and disciplined investment in renewables.

Natural Capital is both the resource base we depend on and the environment we are responsible for. As a lignite and coal-based generator, we manage our impact on air, water, land and biodiversity with care, and we are rebalancing our portfolio towards renewables and clean energy so that we can meet the nation's energy needs more sustainably. Responsible stewardship of natural resources runs through our mining, generation and diversification activities alike.
Our Scope 1 emissions rose modestly in FY 2025-26, in step with higher generation across the group. Our Scope 2 emissions, by contrast, fell sharply to about an eighth of the previous year's level as we drew a far greater share of our auxiliary and administrative power from renewable sources. The direction of these two numbers captures our approach in miniature: The emissions is tied to the power that we generate move with demand, while the emissions within our own control continue to come down.
Efforts towards energy management

Efforts towards energy management
Energy stewardship is an essential pillar of our sustainability strategy, underpinning both prudent use of national energy resources and the efficiency of our own operations. We pursue it through systematic replacement of conventional equipment with energy-efficient alternatives, regular maintenance, and upgrading our in-house expertise. These measures deliver tangible operational gains and build a culture of conservation across our mining and power operations.

Material Issues
Our main lever for reducing greenhouse gas emissions is the steady expansion of our renewable portfolio, so that cleaner generation displaces a growing share of our fossil-based output over time. We are investing over `50,000 crore to scale our renewable capacity from around 1.43 GW to 10.11 GW by 2030, while our corporate target is to reach a 50% renewable share in our portfolio by 2030 and 77% by 2047, supporting India's goal of net-zero emissions by 2070. NATURAL CAPITAL
Green growth and decarbonisation
We have secured a 600 MW solar project at Khavda in Gujarat through a power purchase agreement with Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Limited, and won a 500 MW solar tender from the Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency under the CPSU scheme, with development awarded to Tata Power Solar Systems Limited and Kosol Energie Private Limited. Through joint ventures, we are developing renewable projects at a larger scale still, including a 2,000 MW ultra-mega solar project under formation with TANGEDCO and a 5,000 MW solar programme through our joint venture with Coal India Limited.

Advancing low-cost, low-carbon technologies of energy transition is central to how we plan our growth. We are laying out a decarbonisation roadmap across our operations and infrastructure, carried forward through capacity targets set out in our Corporate Plan 2030 and through our two dedicated green subsidiaries. This work aligns our expansion with India's wider transition to cleaner energy while strengthening the reliability of the power we supply.
Getting deeper into renewables
Integrating green power into operations
By diversifying our energy mix and reducing our carbon footprint, we continue to expand our renewable portfolio at pace, working towards the 10.11 GW target we have set for 2030. We are building this capacity both for our own account and in partnership. We are advancing solar and wind projects across states, including a 150 MW solar-wind hybrid project awarded by the Solar Energy Corporation of India, for which letters of award were issued to Ionx Wind Limited for a 100 MW solar project and to Enerture Technologies Private Limited for a 50 MW wind project.

We have drawn up a strategy with renewables claiming an increasing share of the energy that feeds our sites. We have installed captive solar plants across our townships and complexes, including rooftop solar on our non-residential buildings at Neyveli and a 200 kW floating solar array on the TPS-I lake, and a hybrid wind-solar system at our research centre. Small against the scale of the capacity we build for the grid, these installations reduce the carbon intensity of running our own operations and demonstrate the technologies we deploy at larger scale elsewhere.
Research in green technologies
Diversifying to tap into opportunities
Our energy transition is supported by research into the technologies that will shape it. We have strengthened our collaborations with academic and research institutions, we are carrying forward pilot projects in green hydrogen and in our lignite-to-methanol pathway, and developing advanced carbon capture as part of the agreement with IIT Madras.

Our energy management extends into new businesses built on our core strengths. Our lignite-to-methanol facility offers a route to higher-value products from the resources we mine, consistent with the direction of India's energy transition. We are also exploring opportunities in electric-vehicle infrastructure, where rising demand and supportive government policy create the prospect of charging stations and associated energy- storage facilities along national and state highways, drawing on our combined expertise in solar power generation and battery storage. These opportunities extend the value of our resource base and our capabilities into the business of a cleaner energy economy.
Innovating energy storage
The supply of steady and reliable green power depends on storage. As part of our initiative to build storage capacity in our portfolio, we have rolled out our first large-scale battery energy storage system, a 250 MW/500 MWh project in Tamil Nadu awarded by TANGEDCO, secured through a purchase agreement with the Tamil Nadu Power Distribution Corporation Limited, for which the land agreement has been signed. This project allows us to store renewable generation and release it when the grid needs it most, enabling greater grid stability and the use of clean power we produce.

NATURAL CAPITAL
Air Emissions Our operations chiefly generate particulate matter from excavation, drilling, haulage and storage. Oxides of sulphur and nitrogen and fly ash are produced from combustion in our thermal units. We acknowledge these impacts and address them through control at source, continuous monitoring and a robust framework of compliance.
Water and Effluent Management Our operations, particularly mining and thermal power generation, depend on a rigorous framework that ensures water is used efficiently, treated responsibly, and replenished wherever possible. By continuously improving how we handle water, we aim to protect the ecological balance and safeguard the needs of the communities around us.

Rather than treat that pumped water as waste, we put it to use: the greater part feeds our thermal power stations, and the balance is sent to nearby villages for agricultural use, so that water raised for mining serves generation and farming before it returns to the land. Our total water withdrawal rose during the year, in step with the higher scale of our mining and generation, and the larger share of what we draw continues to be reused rather than discharged.

In our thermal stations, we control emissions through the technology we have built into the plants. Electrostatic precipitators capture particulate matter, our supercritical boilers generate power more efficiently, and we are in the process of adopting flue gas desulphurisation to bring down sulphur emissions further. Our monitored sulphur dioxide readings remained above our desired levels, and the phased introduction of flue gas desulphurisation across our units is the response we are putting in place. We are also pursuing carbon capture at source through our 2025 pact with IIT Madras. The research collaboration is fully funded by us that moves from a laboratory study to a pilot demonstration, tackling carbon dioxide from combustion directly.
Controlling and reducing emissions
In our mining areas, we suppress the dust produced by mining. An extensive water-spraying system covers haul roads, conveyors, working faces, vehicle movement and bunker areas, supported by the practice of wet drilling, so that dust is contained before it can travel. Our electrically operated bucket wheel excavators and belt conveyors, maintained over three decades, keep the carbon load and the emissions of our mining materially lower than that in diesel-based extractions. The three-tier green belts we develop around our bunker and mining areas trap dust while adding to the green cover of the region.

We manage the quality of our water as carefully as the quantity. To control the suspended solids that mining washes into water through seepage and surface run-off, we have constructed siltation wells and weirs along the canals in and around our mines. The wastewater from our operations, from station blowdown, vehicle washing and domestic use, passes through sewage and effluent treatment plants across our sites and townships, and the treated water is returned to use for gardening, greenbelt development, industrial washing and irrigation. Our water and wastewater are sampled and tested every month by the Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board or accredited laboratories, and the results stay within permissible limits.
To check the decline in the pressure surface of the deep confined aquifer, we have also taken up artificial recharge through injection wells, in a global collaboration with Rheinbraun Engineering of Germany and IIT Madras, tested at depths of around 250 metres in the complex aquifer conditions of the Neyveli region. We monitor the resource regionally through observation wells established in consultation with the Central Ground Water Board, and we prepare our water balance from continuous data on pumping, water levels and quality.

Beyond using water well, we work to return it to the ground. Mining is a temporary use of land. At the project formulation stage of every mine, we prepare a comprehensive plan to rehabilitate the land our operations disturb, so that the ground returns to productive use as mining moves on. We backfill the mined-out areas and reclaim them through three complementary methods: physical reclamation by land levelling, dozing and the conservation of topsoil; chemical reclamation using soil amendments and inorganic fertilisers; and biological reclamation using bio-fertilisers, green manure and green leaf manure. The reclaimed land is put to use for agriculture, horticulture, pasture and the development of green belt. Through more than six decades of what we practise as clean and green mining, this reclamation has created a substantial green cover in and around our mining areas.

Cultivation on reclaimed land
We have taken our reclamation a step further, turning mined-out land back to agriculture through collaborative projects under the Ministry of Coal's Science and Technology programme. Under our Hi-Tech cultivation project, run with Annamalai University and Tamil Nadu Agricultural University, we grow vegetables on the inert soils of our mined-out lands at three Neyveli mines using drip irrigation and mulching. In our polyhouses, in collaboration with IISc Bengaluru, we raise high- quality vegetables through hydroponics, an automated, soil-free method that grows produce through a water circulation system. These projects show that land once mined can be returned to agricultural value.
Manufactured sand from overburden

Manufactured sand from overburden
At the centre of our waste management is the principle we practise as waste into wealth: the idea that a material should be used to its fullest before it is ever treated as waste. This philosophy is guided by the 6R approach, refuse, rethink, reduce, repair, reuse and recycle, and it shapes how we handle the largest of our byproducts. Fly ash, the residue of burning lignite and coal, is managed scientifically and channelled to cement and brick manufacturers, so that a byproduct of our generation becomes an input for the construction industry. Our research teams extend the value we draw from fly ash further still, into rare earth elements, geopolymer building materials and high- purity silica, work carried in detail in our Intellectual Capital.
A notable step in our circular-economy work is the conversion of mine overburden into manufactured sand. By processing the overburden from lignite mining into M-Sand, we offer a sustainable substitute for natural river sand, reducing the burden that sand mining places on riverine ecosystems while turning a mining byproduct into a material of value. This work reduces our reliance on natural resources and reinforces the framework of responsible resource management that our waste policy sets out.

Global Economy
Outlook
According to the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) World Economic Outlook, July 2026, global growth is projected to moderate to 3.0% in CY26, before rising to 3.4% in CY27. Renewed geopolitical disruptions, driven largely by the West Asia war are pushing energy prices upwards and disrupting global trade flow, resulting in global inflation to increase to an estimated 4.7% in CY26. However, positive tailwinds include accelerated AI technology investment, ongoing real wage recovery, and accommodative monetary policy frameworks.

Demonstrating strong fundamental resilience, the global economy maintained steady progress throughout CY25 across diverse regional markets and sectors. Worldwide economic output expanded by 3.5%, sustained by underlying momentum as markets successfully adapted to higher interest rates, normalising inflation, and shifting geopolitical dynamics. Advanced economies achieved a stable, sustainable growth pace of 1.9% while balancing tighter monetary frameworks and changing trade flows. However, trade policy uncertainties and potential cost pressures stemming from U.S. tariff impositions continue to cast a shadow over near-term global investment and market stability. Meanwhile, emerging and developing economies continued to serve as powerful growth engines, expanding by 4.5% on the back of vibrant domestic consumption and strategic public investments.

India Economy
Outlook

Outlook
Looking ahead to FY 2026-27, economic growth is expected to remain steady at 6.6%, supported by a revival in urban consumption, aided by direct tax rationalisation, and resilient rural demand, driven by strong agricultural momentum following proactive climate-mitigation measures. Balanced input costs are expected to support corporate margins and fiscal stability, while improved real wages and stabilising core inflation will further lift discretionary spending, a key metric for the auto and retail sectors. The RBI is maintaining a data-dependent, neutral stance, using calibrated liquidity management to ensure price dynamics remain within target while supporting sustainable credit flows. Crucially, robust momentum across core infrastructure sectors, driven by surging electricity demand and expansion in mining, will reinforce high-capacity utilisation and private capital expenditure, fueling sustained long-term industrial momentum.
India’s economy exhibited exceptional resilience in FY 2025-26, successfully navigating global market conditions through steady domestic fundamentals. According to the National Statistical Office (NSO), India’s real GDP grew by a robust 7.7% during the year, underpinned by strong private consumption, vibrant services expansion and sustained public capital spending.

Global price pressures eased noticeably. Headline inflation moderated to 4.1%, supported by proactive monetary policies and stable energy costs during the year. While service sector inflation and policy shifts called for prudent capital allocation, businesses and investors navigated the year with strategic focus and measured confidence.
Over the past four years, average retail inflation, as measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI), has followed a clear downward trajectory, declining steadily from 6.7% in FY 2022-23 to 1.7% in 2025-26. To further nurture growth and support long-term investment momentum alongside easing price pressures, the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) maintained a calibrated easing framework, establishing the policy repo rate at 5.25% following progressive rate adjustments. This monetary flexibility was anchored by benign core inflation, which remained comfortably contained around 3.6%, even as input cost dynamics in key industrial sectors like metals and energy remained closely monitored.

While international market shifts call for strategic adaptability, India’s domestic growth trajectory remains securely anchored. Despite global energy price pressures and supply chain headwind stemming from the West Asia conflict, headline CPI inflation is projected to pick up from a low base of 2.1% in FY 2025-26 to a manageable 5.1% in FY 2026-27, with core inflation remaining well-contained. Quarterly CPI is expected to follow a stable trajectory: 4.2% in Q1, 5.1% in Q2, 5.9% in Q3, and 5.4% in Q4, with inflation risks viewed as broadly balanced. Real GDP expansion across quarters, 6.6% in Q1, 6.3% in Q2, 6.5% in Q3, and 6.8% in Q4, reflects a resilient domestic foundation for durable economic progress.

Grid-India oversees centralised price discovery and uniform market clearing across both the Day-Ahead (DAM) and Real-Time (RTM) electricity markets.
Tax Write-Off & Accelerated Depreciation Rules for Rooftop Solar
India's wind power landscape continues its upward trajectory. Over the past decade, nationwide installed capacity expanded by more than 160%, growing from a 21 GW baseline in FY 2014–15 to 56 GW by FY 2025-26. This expansion was propelled by a landmark single-year addition of 6.05 GW during FY 2025-26.

Solar power leads India's shift toward clean energy. From just 2.82 GW in FY 2014–15, total solar capacity expanded 53.28x to reach 150.26 GW in FY 2025-26. A historic single-year addition of 29.70 GW during the year under review highlights this surging momentum. Today, solar forms the bedrock of the country's renewable energy basket, reinforced by expanding decentralised rooftop systems and a maturing local supply chain. Targeted policy mechanisms, ranging from dedicated solar park infrastructure to enhanced grid connectivity and local module manufacturing under the Make in India initiative, continue to drive this unprecedented scale-up.

Under the self-owned CAPEX model, businesses can claim a 40% Accelerated Depreciation tax deduction under Section 32 in Year 1, significantly lowering taxable income compared to the standard 15% rate. Entities under the Old Tax Regime can add a 20% initial depreciation under Section 32(1)(iia) for a 60% total first-year write-off (unavailable under the 115BAA/115BAB concessional tax regimes). To get the full Year 1 deduction, the plant must be commissioned before October 3 ( 180 days of use). If commissioned after October 3 (<180 days), the allowable first-year claim is halved to 20% under concessional regimes or 30% under the old regime. These write-offs require direct ownership, excluding third-party OPEX/RESCO PPAs, and allow capitalising uncredited GST into the asset base.
Total electricity generated from wind reached 91.40 BU over the same fiscal period, contributing 5.15% to the national power grid. Concurrently, domestic supply chains have matured, with 14 Indian manufacturers now producing 31 type-certified turbine variants. Backed by an annual domestic manufacturing capability of 18 GW, the sector remains well-equipped to drive future onshore and offshore installations.

Driven by the National Critical Mineral Mission (NCMM), critical minerals, including lithium, cobalt, nickel, rare earth elements, and copper, form the strategic backbone of clean energy technologies, powering solar modules, wind turbines, electric vehicles (EVs), grid- scale energy storage systems, and green hydrogen electrolysers.
Energy Storage: Advanced grid-scale energy storage systems rely directly on lithium, cobalt, and nickel.
Solar Energy: Critical minerals such as silicon, tellurium, indium, and gallium are vital for photovoltaic (PV) cell production. India’s current solar capacity of 150.26 GW is heavily dependent on these minerals.

Multipliers for different RE Technologies
Critical minerals are vital for economic development and national security, but geographic concentration creates strategic supply vulnerabilities. To secure self-reliance, the government launched the National Critical Mineral Mission (NCMM) spanning FY 2024-25 to 2030–31. Building on the 30 critical minerals identified by the Ministry of Mines, 24 are listed under Part D of Schedule I of the amended Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 (MMDR Act). Under this framework, the Central Government holds exclusive authority to auction mining leases, composite licenses, and exploration licenses. Under NCMM, over 100 critical mineral blocks are targeted for central auctions to accelerate domestic exploration, processing, and recycling.
Green Hydrogen & Fuel Cells: Critical rare earth elements such as Cerium (Ce), Lanthanum (La), Yttrium (Y), Gadolinium (Gd), Samarium (Sm), Scandium (Sc), Neodymium (Nd) and Praseodymium (Pr) are essential for high-performance green hydrogen production and fuel cell technologies, serving as key materials in electrolytes, electrodes, catalysts and electrolysis systems.
Wind Energy: Rare earth elements like dysprosium and neodymium power wind turbine permanent magnets. India aims to expand its wind capacity from 57 GW to 140 GW by 2030, requiring a steady mineral supply.

Key Highlights of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) (MMDR) Amendment Act, 2026
India achieved 100% census village electrification in April 2018, followed by universal household connectivity under Saubhagya. Advancing SDG 7, India has shifted from basic access to 24x7 reliable power under the Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS), while targeting last-mile tribal homes through PM- JANMAN. Furthermore, initiatives like PM Surya Ghar empower households to generate clean rooftop solar power, reinforcing sustainable and self-reliant energy access nationwide.
India is the world’s third-largest producer and consumer of hydrogen, following China and the United States, with an annual demand of approximately 7.5 Million Metric Tonnes Per Annum (MMTPA), primarily consumed in crude oil refining and fertiliser manufacturing. However, the vast majority remains grey hydrogen produced from fossil fuels via steam methane reforming. With national hydrogen demand expected to increase nearly threefold by 2040, the core priority is transitioning this growth toward green hydrogen produced using renewable energy.

India’s Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) market is poised for transformative growth, driven by the nation’s target of achieving 500 GW of non-fossil energy capacity by 2030 and the critical need for grid stability. According to the National Electricity Plan (NEP 2022–32) released by the Central Electricity Authority (CEA), India’s energy storage capacity requirement is projected to reach 82.37 GWh by FY 2026-27, comprising 47.65 GWh from Pumped Storage Projects (PSP) and 34.72 GWh from BESS. This requirement rises significantly to 411.4 GWh by FY 2031–32 (175.18 GWh from PSP and 236.22 GWh from BESS). Furthermore, the CEA projects that by 2047, storage needs will expand to 2,380 GWh (540 GWh from PSP and 1,840 GWh from BESS) to support India’s Net Zero 2070 target.

Energy intensity measures the volume of energy required to yield one unit of GDP at constant prices, serving as a vital gauge of a nation's macroeconomic efficiency. Meanwhile, Per Capita Energy Consumption (PEC) reflects total annual energy use divided by the mid-year population. While both metrics primarily track conventional energy streams, they can undercount non- conventional energy usage, particularly across rural regions.

In addition to setting clear criteria for prioritising enterprise risks, it explicitly defines the roles and accountabilities of all key personnel. In line with policy guidelines, a sub-board Internal Risk Review Committee evaluates risk exposures every quarter, while the overarching risk assessment and mitigation protocols are regularly examined by the Risk Management Committee, Audit Committee, and the Board of Directors.

Internal Control
The Company has well-established Internal Control Systems and Procedures commensurate with its size. The Company has in place an approved and well laid out manuals for Delegation of Powers (DoP), Purchase, Contracts and HR Manuals. This framework balances the minimisation of debt servicing costs against exchange rate and interest rate fluctuations, fully aligned with the organisation's risk tolerance.

By placing stability and risk containment above speculative profit, the policy protects NLCIL's long-term financial health.

The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has introduced a mandatory reporting framework on Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) parameters through the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR). Under this framework, the top 1,000 listed entities, determined on the basis of market capitalisation, are required to furnish comprehensive disclosures on their ESG practices and performance.
Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013 mandates constitution of the Corporate Social Responsibility (“CSR”) Committee.
During the FY 2025-26, the Committee comprised of Four (4) Directors viz. Shri. M.T. Ramesh, Independent Director as the Chairperson and Dr. Suresh Chandra Suman, Shri. M. Venkatachalam and Dr. Prasanna Kumar Acharya, Executive Directors, as its Members.

As on 31st March, 2026, all the Independent Directors ceased to be directors on the Board of the Company w.e.f. 28th March, 2026, consequent to expiry of their term. In order to comply with the provisions of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015, the Ministry of Coal (MoC), Administrative Ministry, is being periodically apprised with regard to the requirement of appointing requisite number of Independent Directors on the Board of the Company. The Ministry of Coal, the Administrative Ministry, has been requested to expedite the appointment of the required number of Independent Directors so as to comply with the applicable guidelines.
In this context, the Company has voluntarily constituted a Board Level ESG Committee to oversee its ESG objectives, monitor progress on ESG related initiatives, and guide the adoption of sustainable business practices, including measures to address climate change and to provide long-term value for all stakeholders.

7. Trade Receivables Management: The Company continued to prioritize receivables management throughout the year. As at 31st March 2026, trade receivables aggregated to ₹ 3,337.69 Crore, which included unbilled revenue of ₹ 1,511.26 Crore subsequently invoiced after the reporting date. On excluding unbilled revenue, net receivables equate to nearly 38 days of revenue from operations, evidencing the robustness of the Company’s billing framework and the rigor maintained in collection practices.
The NLCIL MoU for FY 2025-26 was signed between the Ministry of Coal and NLCIL on a consolidated basis. During the year, your Company delivered a resilient performance across major parameters. The key achievements against the targets of the MoU 2025-26 are as follows:
8. Research & Development and Innovation: During the year, an expenditure ₹ 44.53 Crore was incurred on R&D, representing 1.55% of the Average PBT.
1. Coal Production and Power Generation: NLCIL achieved a consolidated coal production of 19.14 Million Tonnes (MT). The consolidated power generation achieved was 28,944.71 Million Units (MU). During FY 2025-26, the power surrender in respect of NLCIL and Its Subsidiaries is 6,487.58 MU. Considering the power surrender, the power generation for FY 2025-26 is 35,432.29 MU.

9. Shareholder Value Creation and Market Performance: NLCIL's market capitalization has improved from ₹33,926.84 crore at the close of the previous FY to ₹37,245.06 crore at the end of the current FY. In addition to capital appreciation, the company has paid a total of ₹707.18 crore as dividends, achieving a Total Returns to Shareholders (TRS) of 11.86%.
2. Revenue from Operations: NLCIL Group achieved a Revenue from Operations of ₹ 17,489.53 Crore during the financial year.
3. Financial Strength and Ratios: NLCIL maintains a robust financial risk profile, supported by prudent capital deployment, steady internal cash generation, adequate liquidity, and a comfortable debt-servicing position.
10. Employee Health and Safety Initiatives: NLCIL conducted Initial Medical Examinations (IME) for 3,197 employees and contract workmen at the time of recruitment and engagement, with a percentage achievement of 100%. c. A brief on types of customers
The Company caters to a diverse customer base by providing energy and auxiliary services to state distribution companies. The Company also has a fuel supply contract with TAQA Neyveli Power Company Pvt. Ltd., Neyveli, an independent power producer, for its thermal power plant, along with an MoU with NTPC for a period of five years and with DVC for one year for the supply of coal to its thermal power plants. Lignite is sold through the e-auction route to industries for power generation, refractories, and other allied uses. NLCIL is also engaged in power trading, under which commercial enterprises, industrial consumers and power consumers purchase power surrendered by DISCOMs. Coal produced from the Talabira mines is also sold through the e-auction route to power sector consumers, including those in the Non-Regulated Sector (NRS).

The Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) acts as the supervisory body for managing the tariff structures of power generation companies that are under the ownership or control of the Central Government. Power plants are mandated to lodge applications for tariff determination, which may include generating tariff applications, miscellaneous applications, or review applications. When there are objections to the decisions rendered by the Central and State Electricity Regulatory Commissions, the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL) steps in as a specialised appellate authority with expertise across multiple disciplines. Established in 2005, APTEL’s primary responsibility is to adjudicate appeals, which are typically initiated by Distribution Companies (DISCOMs) or power generation stations, especially concerning disputes over capacity and energy charges that CERC may have rejected. The appeal procedure entails the filing of legal documents, known as pleadings, followed by a series of hearings. After the hearings, APTEL may decide to send the case back to the CERC for additional review and to ensure adherence to its directives.

Our audit involves performing procedures to obtain audit evidence about the adequacy of the internal financial controls system over financial reporting and their operating effectiveness. Our audit of internal financial controls over financial reporting included obtaining an understanding of internal financial controls over financial reporting, assessing the risk that a material weakness exists, and testing and evaluating the design and operating effectiveness of internal control based on the assessed risk. We believe that the audit evidence we have obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for our audit opinion on the Company’s internal financial controls system over financial reporting.
Meaning of Internal Financial Controls Over Financial Reporting
A company's internal financial control over financial reporting is a process designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of financial reporting and the preparation of financial statements for external purposes in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles. A company's internal financial control over financial reporting includes those policies and procedures that

(1) pertain to the maintenance of records that, in reasonable detail, accurately and fairly reflect the transactions and dispositions of the assets of the company;
(2) provide reasonable assurance that transactions are recorded as necessary to permit preparation of financial statements in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, and that receipts and expenditures of the company are being made only in accordance with authorisations of management and directors of the company; and
(3) provide reasonable assurance regarding prevention or timely detection of unauthorised acquisition, use, or disposition of the company's assets that could have a material effect on the financial statements.
Inherent Limitations of Internal Financial Controls Over Financial Reporting
Because of the inherent limitations of internal financial controls over financial reporting, including the possibility of collusion or improper management override of controls, material misstatements due to error or fraud may occur and not be detected. Also, projections of any evaluation of the internal financial controls over financial reporting to future periods are subject to the risk that the internal financial control over financial reporting may become inadequate because of changes in conditions, or that the degree of compliance with the policies or procedures may deteriorate.

The lease liability is measured at amortised cost using the effective interest method. At inception of a contract, the Company assesses whether a contract is, or contains, a lease as per the requirements under Ind AS 116. Contingent liabilities are disclosed when there is (i) a possible obligation arising from past events, the existence of which will be confirmed only by the occurrence or non-occurrence of one or more uncertain future events not wholly within the control of the Company or (ii) a present obligation that arises from past events where it is either not probable that an outflow of resources will be required to settle the obligation or a reliable estimate of the amount cannot be made.
At inception or on reassessment of a contract that contains a lease component, the Company allocates the consideration in the contract to each lease component on the basis of their relative stand-alone prices and aggregate standalone prices of non-lease components. Pursuant to Para 57 of Ind AS 19, accounting by an entity for defined benefit plans, inter-alia, involves determining the amount of the net defined benefit liability (asset) which shall be adjusted for any effect of limiting a net defined benefit asset to the asset ceiling prescribed in Para 64. As per Para 64 of Ind AS 19, in case of surplus in a defined benefit plan, an entity shall measure the net defined benefit asset at the lower of actual surplus or the value of the assets ceiling determined using the discount rate. The asset ceiling is the present value of any economic benefits available in the form of refunds from the plan or reductions in future contributions to the plan. The Company adopts a policy of hedging a portion of its estimated foreign currency exposure in respect of forecast transactions over the loan tenure. The Company uses a call spread option strategy consisting of purchased and written foreign currency call options to hedge its currency risk. These contracts are generally designated as cash flow hedges. The Company designates the intrinsic value of the call spread option strategy as the hedging instrument and applies a hedge ratio of 1:1. Changes in the time value of the call spread option strategy are excluded from the designation of the hedging instrument and are separately accounted for as cost of hedging, which is recognised in other equity under the Cost of Hedging Reserve. The Company’s policy is for the critical terms of the call spread option strategy to align with those of the hedged item.

The Company determines the existence of an economic relationship between the hedging instrument and the hedged item based on the currency, amount and timing of their respective cash flows. The Company assesses whether the derivative designated in each hedging relationship is expected to be, and has been, effective in offsetting changes in the cash flows of the hedged item using the hypothetical derivative method.

In these hedge relationships, the main sources of ineffectiveness are:
• the effect of the counterparty’s and the Company’s own credit risk on the fair value of the call spread option strategy, which is not reflected in the change in the fair value of the hedged cash flows attributable to changes in exchange rates; and
• changes in the timing of the hedged transactions.

3. Reasons and Remedial Actions: These deviations were largely attributable to delays in appointment of requisite Independent Directors by the Government of India. Being a Government Company, the power to appoint Directors on the Board of the Company vests with the President of India. The Ministry of Coal (the Administrative Ministry) has been periodically apprised regarding the requirement of appointing the requisite number of Independent Directors, including a Woman Director. Three Independent Directors (Shri. M. T. Ramesh, Dr. Vasant Ashok Patil, and Shri. Pradeep Kumar Saraogi) were appointed by the Ministry of Coal around March 2025 to address the compliance gap. However, these directors completed their one-year term and ceased to hold office on March 27, 2026, creating a recurring compliance challenge. The Company continues to coordinate with the Ministry of Coal for timely appointment of Independent Directors to ensure sustained compliance.

Pursuant to Para 57 of Ind AS 19, accounting by an entity for defined benefit plans, inter-alia, involves determining the amount of the net defined benefit liability (asset) which shall be adjusted for any effect of limiting a net defined benefit asset to the asset ceiling prescribed in Para 64. As per Para 64 of Ind AS 19, in case of surplus in a defined benefit plan, an entity shall measure the net defined benefit asset at the lower of actual surplus or the value of the assets ceiling determined using the discount rate. The asset ceiling is the present value of any economic benefits available in the form of refunds from the plan or reductions in future contributions to the plan. Risk management framework

Risk management framework
The Group has a comprehensive Integrated Risk Management Policy and Framework approved by the Board. Besides risk prioritisation, the roles and responsibilities of the concerned personnel/committees are clearly defined. As per the policy, the Internal Risk Review Committee (below Board level) reviews the risks on a quarterly basis. The risk assessment together with the mitigation procedures is periodically reviewed by the Risk Management Committee, Audit Committee and the Board.
Note 50 Capital management
The Group 's policy is to maintain a strong capital base so as to maintain investor, creditor and market confidence and to sustain future development of the business. Management monitors the return on capital, as well as the level of dividends to equity shareholders.

The Group 's policy is to maintain a strong capital base so as to maintain investor, creditor and market confidence and to sustain future development of the business. Management monitors the return on capital, as well as the level of dividends to equity shareholders.
The Group has framed a comprehensive Foreign Exchange Risk Management Policy (FERMP) to prudently manage the risks associated with its foreign currency borrowings. The policy seeks to strike a balance between optimising the cost of borrowings and mitigating currency and interest rate risks in line with the Group’s risk appetite. The key objectives of the policy are to identify, measure and monitor foreign exchange and interest rate exposures on a periodic basis, adopt selective hedging strategies to reduce risks to acceptable levels, and ensure that decisions are aligned with the overall risk management framework. The policy focuses on risk mitigation and financial stability rather than profit maximisation, thereby safeguarding the Group’s long-term financial sustainability.
The Board of Directors seeks to maintain a balance between the higher returns that might be possible with higher levels of borrowing and the advantages and security afforded by a sound capital position.

Market risk is the risk that changes in market prices, such as foreign exchange rates, interest rates and equity prices, will affect the Group’s income or the value of its holdings of financial instruments. The objective of market risk management is to manage and control market risk exposures within acceptable parameters while optimising returns.
Master netting or similar agreements
The Group enters into derivative transactions under International Swaps and Derivatives Association (ISDA) master netting agreements. In general, under these agreements the amounts owed by each counterparty on a single day in respect of all transactions outstanding in the same currency are aggregated into a single net amount that is payable by one party to the other. In certain circumstances, e.g. when a credit event such as a default occurs, all outstanding transactions under the agreement are terminated, the termination value is assessed and only a single net amount is payable in settlement of all transactions.

STATUTORY AUDIT An independent audit of financial statements is one of the foundations for the effective operation of the capital markets. Quality of audit is vital for maintaining trust in the financial reporting process and the integrity of financial information. We provide our service as statutory auditors of Government organizations, Banks and private sector and public sector companies in various industries. We help clients strengthen internal systems, maintain investor confidence, and comply with statutory obligations that results in enhanced financial discipline.
TAXATION We offer comprehensive tax advisory and compliance solutions under Income Tax, GST, and other fiscal laws. Our services include tax planning, return filing, assessment representation, and advisory on complex transactions. By ensuring timely compliance and efficient tax structuring, we help our clients minimize tax exposure while remaining fully compliant with statutory requirements. Our clients ranges from individual to big organizations including Banks.

MANAGEMENT CONSULTANCY Our management consultancy services assist businesses in achieving operational efficiency and sustained growth. We provide strategic insights on corporate governance, cost control, budgeting, and organizational restructuring. By analyzing financial data and business processes, we offer actionable recommendations to enhance profitability, streamline decision-making, and align business operations with long-term goals. We also assist in creating SOPs and compliance manuals for large Public Sector undertakings.
INTERNAL AUDIT Internal audits focus on improving business controls, risk management, and process efficiency. Our audit team evaluates internal systems to identify inefficiencies, assess risk exposure, and provide recommendations for improvement. Driven by analytics and compliance insights, our internal audit approach promotes accountability and business resilience. This proactive approach helps organizations prevent financial irregularities, comply with internal policies, and drive continuous improvement in governance and operational performance.
